title: Nothing softer than water
hookLine: nothing is softer than water, yet nothing beats it for wearing down the hard (Tao Te Ching 78)
tomorrow: keep your half of the tally

cards: Pick a stone out of a streambed and turn it over in your hand. It's smooth and rounded, with no sharp edge left. Nobody sanded it or hammered it.
The stream did that, flowing over and around it, season after season. Water never pushed hard on that stone; it just never stopped.

Back on day one thousand thirty-nine, chapter eight likened the highest excellence to water. Chapter seventy-eight of the Tao Te Ching looks at water's quiet winning, and then admits something uncomfortable.

teach.h: SOFTEST, YET IT WEARS THE HARD.

teach.b: Nothing under heaven is softer or weaker than water, the chapter says, yet for wearing down what's hard and strong, nothing does better; nothing can take its place. Water doesn't win by becoming hard.
It wins by staying water. Second, the admission. The weak overcomes the strong, the soft overcomes the hard.

There's no one in the world who doesn't know this, the chapter says, and no one who can put it into practice. That's honest: the lesson isn't hidden, just hard to live. When pushed, the reflex is to push back harder.
Whoever takes on the dirt of the country is fit to tend its altars; whoever takes on its misfortunes is fit to rule under heaven.
Like water, which flows to the low, dirty places and carries what others won't, the one who leads is the one who absorbs.
Fourth, the last line: straight words seem backward. Some readers hear the whole book in it.
Soft wins. Low leads. Giving keeps.
It sounds upside down, and the chapter knows it.

Day to day, water's way is persistence without force: practicing the hard piece for a few minutes each day instead of attacking it once, showing up kindly to the same difficult person again, saying the true thing gently, and again next week.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-eight's water as a picture of gentle persistence: the soft wears down the hard, and the one who takes on what others won't is the one fit to lead.

games.q: what does “nothing softer than water” mean?
o: water: the softest thing, yet best at wearing the hard
the gentle rain that farmers prayed for in a drought
a rule that the sage must drink only plain water

p: softest, yet it wears down the hard
whoever takes on the country's dirt

s: chapter seventy-eight says the lesson of water is hidden from most people
it says no one doesn't know it; the trouble is no one can practice it.
the chapter says the one who takes on the country's misfortunes is fit to rule
like water, the leader is the one who takes on what others won't.
the chapter ends: straight words seem backward
soft wins, low leads, and it sounds upside down.

games.q: you face something hard and strong. according to chapter seventy-eight, what wears it down best?
o: water, the softest thing there is.
games.why: nothing is softer or weaker than water, yet nothing does better against the hard and strong. nothing can take its place.

practice: Let the breath move like water, without effort, just continuing, and bring to mind one hard thing you've been pushing against: a skill, a habit, a stuck conversation.
Instead of a big push, think of the stream on the stone, and find one small, gentle thing you could do toward it, almost too small. Rest with the feeling of slow, steady pressure that doesn't strain.
